transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi. Yeah, nice to meet you too. Um... well, I guess I'm here because... I've just been having a really hard time lately with, well, with myself, honestly. We bought this house a little while ago, and I was the one who really pushed for it, you know? I took on this mortgage thinking, 'Oh, I can just pick up more shifts at the restaurant, I can hustle, I can provide for us.' But lately, I just keep feeling like I’ve completely let my family down by taking on this massive debt. It's like this constant, heavy weight, just sitting on my chest from the second I wake up. I look at my wife and I just think about how I've trapped us and how I'm failing them. 

And it’s getting to the point where it’s spilling over into everything else, especially my job. I mean, I wait tables, right? It’s not rocket science, I've got some college under my belt, I should be able to handle it. But every single time I make a small mistake—like forgetting to put in a side of dressing or putting in the wrong drink order—it just... it hits me so incredibly hard. I don't just brush it off like a normal person. It just proves to me that I’m completely useless. It’s not just a mistake, it’s like this glaring proof that I'm a failure and I deserve whatever bad things happen to me, whatever financial ruin comes our way. I just can't stop feeling so incredibly guilty about all of it, just constantly replaying every little screw-up and thinking about how I'm dragging everyone down with me... I just don't know how to turn it off.
Have you been having thoughts that you’d be better off dead or of hurting yourself?

Well, it's... it's a heavy question, you know? And I want to be completely honest with you because I really do need help. I'm not... I don't have a plan. I want to be really clear about that. I'm not sitting around figuring out a way to hurt myself or, you know, end it all. I don't have a plan to do anything like that. But... the thoughts do creep in. It's usually at night, or really early in the morning. Like, before one of my early shifts at the restaurant. I'll be lying there in bed, staring at the ceiling, listening to my wife breathe next to me, and the weight of the mortgage and all my screw-ups just starts pressing down on me so hard. 

And in those moments, when it's so quiet and I'm just trapped in my own head with all this guilt, I do sometimes think... I think about how much easier it would be if I just didn't wake up. If I could just close my eyes and everything would stop. The worrying, the failing, the constant feeling that I'm ruining their lives... it would all just be over. I wouldn't have to go into work and mess up another order and feel like an idiot again. I wouldn't have to look at the bills. It just feels like it would be a relief, you know? Just... not having to keep failing at everything. It's not that I want to actively do something to make it happen, but the idea of just slipping away and not having to face another day of being me... it definitely crosses my mind more than I'd like to admit.
Did these feelings start after you took on the mortgage and bought the house?

Yeah, exactly. Well, it’s a condo, actually, but yes. If I really sit down and think about the exact timeline, it’s been going on for about a year and eight months now. 

I remember it so clearly because we had just gone through that whole grueling process, you know? The inspections, the endless paperwork, sitting in that little office signing my name on a million dotted lines. And for a second—maybe just a few days—I felt like I had really done something good. But then, almost as soon as we started unpacking boxes and the reality of the monthly payments set in, that's when it all shifted. So it's been a solid year and eight months of this. 

I can almost picture the exact moment the first mortgage statement arrived in the mail. I opened it up, looked at the balance, and it was like all the air just left the room. Ever since then, for these last twenty months or so, it's just been this incredibly heavy burden. I thought I was stepping up, getting us this condo, but instead, I just started feeling this intense, crushing guilt that hasn't let up since. Every single day for a year and eight months, just waking up and realizing that the debt is still there, and that I'm the one who did this to us. So, yeah, it definitely traces right back to taking on that mortgage.
Do you believe your family would actually be better off without you because of the debt you took on?

I mean... I don't know. It's... it's hard to say if they'd actually be better off, like, in reality. Because, you know, my wife and I, we've been together a long time. She tells me she loves me, and we've been through a lot together, way back since I was just taking a few college classes and starting out in the service industry. So emotionally, I guess... I guess it would hurt her. I know it would. I'm not trying to cause her pain. 

But... financially? And just, like, the burden of it all? That's where my brain just gets completely stuck. I'll be at the restaurant, at the end of the night, just rolling silverware or wiping down the stations, my feet are just completely aching, my shirt smells like fry oil, and I just start running the numbers in my head. I think about how she was perfectly fine renting. She actually liked our old place, you know, even with the loud neighbors and the terrible parking situation. She was happy. But I was the one who had to push for this condo. I had to be the guy who provides a home, the one who steps up. 

So when I look at the reality of it now, the debt... sometimes I really do think that if I just wasn't in the picture, she could just sell the place, downsize, and just... be free of this massive mistake I forced on us. I don't know for absolute sure if she'd be better off, and she'd probably tell you no if you asked her, but... in my head, especially when things get really dark and quiet, it just feels like I'm this anchor pulling her underwater. It's just this constant debate I have with myself, over and over, trying to figure out if my being here is doing more harm than good, and I just can't seem to convince myself that I'm actually worth the trouble I've caused.
Aside from the mortgage and your mistakes at work, do you find yourself worrying a lot about many other things in your life?

Not really... no. It's actually kind of strange when you think about it, because you'd think with everything going on in the world, or just normal everyday stuff, I'd have a list of worries a mile long. But it's really just... it's just the condo and work. It's like my brain only has a certain amount of space, or bandwidth, I guess, and that space is completely maxed out by the mortgage and how much I'm screwing up at the restaurant. 

Like, just the other week, the check engine light came on in my car—it's an older Civic, we've had it forever, and usually, something like that would send me into a panic about repair costs or how I'm going to get to my shifts. But I just looked at the dashboard and felt... nothing. I didn't even care. My wife asked me if we needed to take it to the shop, and I just shrugged. Because in the grand scheme of things, a broken car doesn't even register compared to this massive, crushing debt I've strapped us to. 

So, no, I don't really sit around worrying about my health, or the news, or the future in general, or anything like that. It's just this constant, looping track of 'how are we going to pay for this place' and 'why did I mess up that order for table six.' It just loops and loops. I'll be standing at the POS system at work, punching in an order, and instead of worrying about the lunch rush or the angry customers, I'm just doing the math on our property taxes in my head. It's so specific, you know? It's just those two things—the house and my failures at work—playing on repeat. Nothing else really even manages to break through that noise anymore.
Over this past year and eight months, have you felt down or depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Yeah... yeah, I have. It’s hard to even describe it properly because it’s not just being sad, you know? It’s like... most days there’s this heavy, empty feeling sitting right in the middle of my chest. Just this weight. And it’s been there pretty much every single day since this whole thing started. 

I’ll be at the restaurant, and I’m carrying trays of plates, refilling water glasses, doing the whole routine. And I’m smiling at the customers, saying, "How is everything tasting tonight?" or "Can I get you some more bread?" because, well, I have to. That’s the job. But I’m just going through the motions. I’m smiling because I’m supposed to, not because I actually feel anything good or pleasant inside. It’s like I’m a robot just executing a program, but inside, underneath the apron and the fake smile, it’s just... hollow. 

And it doesn’t really lift when I go home, either. I’ll walk through the door of the condo—the condo that started all of this—and my wife will ask how my shift was, and I’ll just say "fine," but that heavy feeling is still right there in my chest. It’s there when I wake up, it’s there when I’m tying my shoes for work, it’s there when I’m wiping down tables at midnight. It’s just this constant, dull ache that never really goes away. So, yeah, nearly every day for the last year and eight months, it’s just been this overwhelming, heavy emptiness. I can’t seem to shake it no matter what I do or how hard I try to just put on a brave face for my tables or my wife.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

I don't... I don't really know if I have. It's hard to tell, honestly. I mean, my wife and I used to go out to the movies sometimes on my days off, or we'd go for a hike up at the state park when the weather was nice. We'd pack a lunch, just some sandwiches and fruit, and spend the whole afternoon out there. And I used to really like doing that. It felt good to get out of the city and just breathe some fresh air, you know? Away from the restaurant, away from the smells and the noise. 

But lately, we just haven't been doing any of that. And I don't know if it's because I've lost interest in those things, or if it's just because I'm so exhausted all the time from working extra shifts to try and pay down the mortgage, or if it's because every time I think about spending even a little bit of money on a movie ticket or gas to drive to the park, I just feel this incredible guilt. Like, how can I justify spending money on fun when we're drowning in this debt? So we just stay home. 

And when I'm home, I just sit on the couch. I used to read a bit—mostly sci-fi paperbacks, nothing too heavy—but now I'll pick up a book and read the same paragraph five times without absorbing a single word because my brain is just doing the math on the property taxes again. So I put the book down. Is that losing interest? Or is it just being distracted? I really couldn't tell you. I just know that nothing feels the same anymore. Even the food at the restaurant, the stuff I used to think was pretty good, it all just tastes like cardboard to me now. I don't know if that's what you mean, but... yeah, I guess I just don't really do much of anything for fun these days. It just doesn't seem like there's any room for it.
When these thoughts about the mortgage and your mistakes come up, do they feel intrusive and unwanted, like they pop into your mind against your will?

Intrusive? I don't... I wouldn't really use that word. It's not like they just suddenly jump out of nowhere and surprise me, or like they're against my will. It's more like... they're just the reality of my situation, you know? Like, the mortgage is a real thing. The papers are sitting right there on the kitchen counter at home, right next to the toaster. We have this old silver toaster that barely works anymore, you have to push the lever down twice to get it to catch, and the stack of bills and the mortgage statements are just piled right there next to it. So it's not like my brain is making up some random, unwanted thought out of the blue. It's just my life. 

I'm thinking about it because I feel like I *have* to think about it. If I don't figure out how we're going to pay for this condo, who will? My wife is already stressed enough with her own stuff. So I'm just constantly mulling it over. It's not against my will, it's just... what else is there to think about? 

Like I said before, I'll be at the POS terminal at the restaurant, and I'll be punching in an order—like yesterday, this guy wanted the grilled salmon but with the dill sauce on the side and asparagus instead of the roasted potatoes, which is a two-dollar upcharge, by the way, and I almost forgot to ring in the upcharge, which would have been yet another stupid mistake for my manager to get on my case about. But the whole time I'm punching that complicated order in, the math about the mortgage is just running in the background. It doesn't pop into my head because it never really leaves my head, if that makes sense. It's just the baseline now. It's like a radio left on in the next room. You don't always focus on the exact song playing, but you know the radio is on and you can hear the bass thumping. 

So, no, I wouldn't say they pop in against my will or anything like that. I'm just trying to solve a problem that feels completely impossible to solve, and my brain just keeps working on it, over and over.
Before you bought the condo, had you ever gone through a period like this in your life?

No... no, never. I mean, sure, I’d get stressed sometimes, like if we had a crazy Mother's Day brunch rush at the restaurant and we were short a server and the kitchen was backed up on tickets, but it was just normal stress. You clock out, you go home, you sleep it off, and it's gone. Nothing at all like *this*. 

This specific feeling... this whole heavy, empty situation where my brain just won't stop, it’s really only been going on for about a year and eight months. It started exactly after I took on the condo mortgage. I can trace it right back to that very week, honestly. 

Before that, my wife and I were just renting this little one-bedroom place over on the west side. It wasn't anything fancy, the radiator made this terrible clanking noise in the winter and the carpet was this ugly beige color, but it was manageable, you know? The rent was cheap. We didn't have this massive financial anvil hanging over our heads. But then we decided we needed to buy, because everyone always tells you that renting is just throwing money away, right? Everyone says real estate is the smart move. 

So we found this condo, and we sat down in that title office... I still remember the room, it was way too cold, and the broker had this ridiculous, massive mahogany desk, and he just kept sliding paper after paper across to me. "Sign here, initial here, date this one." And I did. I just kept signing. But almost the second the ink dried on that final mortgage document, it was like the reality of what I had just done hit me. The sheer amount of money I was suddenly on the hook for. It was like this physical weight just dropped right onto my chest before we even left the parking lot of the title company. 

So, no, before that day, I was a pretty regular guy. I could actually sit down and enjoy my days off. It’s just been this last year and eight months, ever since that mortgage became my responsibility, that everything just shifted and I haven't been able to get back to how I used to be.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

I wouldn't say I have trouble sleeping, no. Actually, it's almost the opposite in a way, just because of how physically exhausted I am by the time I actually get into bed. You see, working at the restaurant, especially since I've been picking up all these extra shifts to try and make a dent in the condo payments, I'm on my feet for ten, sometimes twelve hours a day. We have to wear these specific black, non-slip shoes because it's company policy, and let me tell you, they have absolutely zero arch support. None. 

So by the time I finally clock out, do all my side work—rolling silverware, wiping down the wait station, making sure the coffee machines are totally broken down and cleaned out so the morning crew doesn't complain about us—by the time all that is done and I take the bus home, my legs feel like they're made of lead. 

When I get home, I don't even really have the energy to stay awake and worry, even if I wanted to. I just take off my uniform, leave it in a pile by the laundry basket because I'm too tired to even put it in the machine, and I just collapse. We have this queen-size mattress we bought a few years ago, back when things were simpler and we were just renting, and it sags a little bit on my side, but I honestly don't even care. The second my head hits the pillow, I'm just out. It's like this heavy, dead sleep. Sometimes my wife will still be up, watching TV in the living room—she likes those baking competition shows, the ones where they make the really elaborate cakes—and I can hear the muffled sound of the TV through the drywall, but it doesn't bother me at all. I just sleep right through it. 

So, no, getting to sleep isn't really an issue for me. The sleeping part is fine. It's more... it's the waking up part that's hard. Because the second I open my eyes in the morning, before I even sit up, my brain just instantly boots up and remembers the mortgage and the debt and the whole mess. And then that physical weight is just right back on my chest for the rest of the day. But the actual sleeping? No, I don't have any trouble with that. I'm just too wiped out to stay awake.
Have you been having trouble concentrating?

Yeah... yeah, I actually have been. It's becoming a real issue at the restaurant, to be honest. Like I was saying earlier about the POS terminal... I've been doing this for years, right? I know that computer system inside and out. It's this older touchscreen setup, the screen is always a little greasy no matter how much we wipe it down with the sanitizer rags, but usually, I can punch in a massive order for a six-top in my sleep. 

But lately? I'm just having so much trouble keeping the numbers straight. I'll be standing there at the POS, or doing the end-of-night inventory sheets—which is a whole other thing, my manager has me counting the liquor bottles and the dry goods in the back storage room where it's always freezing cold and smells like industrial bleach—and I'll just find myself staring at the screen or the clipboard. I’ll look at the numbers I just typed in, and even though I know I've done this exact same task a thousand times, I just don't trust what I just entered. 

I have to stop and ask myself, wait, did I ring in table 42 or 24? Did I count four backup bottles of the house Cabernet or five? And I'll just stand there, staring at the glowing screen, and my brain just kind of... blanks out. It's like the gears just stop turning. I end up having to delete the whole order and start over just to be safe, which obviously takes up more time, and then the kitchen expeditor starts yelling for me to run hot food for someone else's section, which just makes me lose my place all over again. So yeah, my focus is just completely shot right now.
Since this started, has there been any period of at least 2 months when you felt back to your usual self?

No... no, definitely not two months. I mean, I really wish I could say yes, but honestly, since that day at the title office, it's just been one long, continuous stretch of this heavy feeling. 

You know, working in the restaurant business, you kind of measure time in seasons and rushes. Like, you have the crazy holiday rush in December where everyone is ordering the expensive steaks and the good wine, and you're making decent tips but you're running yourself ragged. And then January hits and it's dead quiet, and you're just standing around the wait station polishing the same wine glasses over and over because there's nobody at the tables. Then you get the spring patio season, which is a whole different kind of chaos because everyone wants to sit outside even if it's still fifty degrees out... 

Anyway, I've been through almost two full cycles of all those seasons since we bought the condo, and at no point during any of them did I ever feel like I was back to my old self. Not for two months, not even for two weeks, really. 

I mean, sure, maybe I'll have a good shift here and there. Like, maybe a table is really nice and they leave me a fifty-dollar tip on a hundred-dollar check, and for about ten minutes on the bus ride home, I'll look out the window and think, "Okay, maybe we can breathe a little bit. Maybe this isn't so bad." But it never lasts. The second I walk through the front door, or the second I wake up the next morning and remember the mortgage payment that's coming up on the first of the month... boom. It's right back. The exact same crushing weight on my chest, just instantly. 

So, a whole two months of feeling normal? Like the guy I was before we bought the place, who could actually relax on a Tuesday afternoon? No. Not even close. It's just been this constant, unbroken line of it ever since the day we signed those papers.
Have you noticed that your appetite has gone down?

Well, it's not exactly that it's just gone down, no. It’s more like... my eating has just been completely all over the place. 

You know how it works in the restaurant industry, they usually give us what we call "family meal" or staff meal before the dinner rush starts, usually around four-thirty or five o'clock. The prep cooks will just throw together this massive metal hotel pan of baked ziti or chicken scraps over rice, you know, whatever ingredients they need to use up before the weekend food truck delivery comes in. And usually, I’d eat a huge plate of it because you never know when you'll actually get to stop and eat again during a ten-hour shift. 

But lately, some weeks I just... I barely touch the staff meal. I'll look at this big pan of heavy food sitting under the heat lamps in the back hallway and I just have absolutely zero desire to put it in my mouth. My stomach just feels like it's tied in a knot, probably from thinking about the condo payments or the credit cards, and I can't even force a single bite down. I'll just drink a bunch of ice water from the fountain and go fold napkins or stock the ice bins instead. 

But then, it swings completely the other way. I'll get through the entire shift running on basically nothing, take the bus back, and walk into our place at like one in the morning. And suddenly, I'll just go into the kitchen, leave the overhead lights off so I don't wake up my wife, and I'll just eat whatever is in the kitchen. And I'm not even really doing it because my stomach is growling, it's more like... I just eat it to feel settled. Like I'll stand there in front of the open fridge in the dark
Have you lost or gained a noticeable amount of weight during this time?

Well, yeah, I guess that's the thing about how my eating has been so all over the place, like I was just saying. Because some weeks I barely touch that staff meal, like I mentioned, and then other nights I come home and just eat whatever's in the kitchen just to feel settled... it definitely shows on the scale. 

I actually noticed it the other day when I was getting dressed for my shift. We have these uniform pants, right? They're just basic black slacks, poly-blend, nothing fancy, we have to buy them ourselves from this uniform supply store downtown. And I've had the same three pairs in rotation for, I don't know, maybe four years now. I know exactly how they fit. But lately, I've been having to cinch my belt a full notch tighter, sometimes two notches, depending on the week. 

At first, I thought maybe they shrank in the wash, even though they're polyester and shouldn't shrink, but then I realized, no, it's me. Because when I go through those periods where I'm just too stressed to eat, where the thought of the mortgage just completely kills my appetite and I'm just drinking ice water all shift... I definitely drop weight. I can feel it in my face, you know? Like my cheekbones feel sharper when I wash my face at night. 

But then, when I have those nights where I'm standing in the dark kitchen at 1 AM eating half a loaf of bread and whatever else I can find just to calm my nerves down enough to sleep... the weight comes back on. It's like this constant yo-yo effect. I'll lose maybe five or six pounds over a couple of weeks when things are really bad and I can't stomach the thought of food, and then I'll put it right back on, plus maybe a little extra, when I get into those late-night stress-eating phases. 

So it's not like I've steadily gained twenty pounds or steadily lost twenty pounds. It's more like my weight is just constantly fluctuating up and down by five to eight pounds, back and forth, depending on which way my appetite is swinging that week. It's really frustrating, honestly, because my uniform pants never fit right anymore. They're either sagging off my waist or they feel uncomfortably tight after a few days of late-night eating. So yeah, there's definitely been a noticeable change, just... in both directions, if that makes sense.
If the condo were no longer a problem tomorrow, do you think this heavy depressed feeling would go away?

I mean... I really don't know. I have thought about that a lot, actually. Like, if we just put the place on the market and sold it, or if some magic wand waved and the mortgage was suddenly paid off, would I just wake up and be completely fine? 

But honestly, I don't think it would just vanish overnight. Because at this point, it feels like it has become more than just the stress about the money or the building itself. It has kind of settled deep into me. Most days, there is just this heavy, empty feeling right here in the center of my chest. It is almost like a physical weight, just sitting there from the moment I wake up until I finally fall asleep. 

And I go to work, and I am really just going through the motions. I am carrying these massive ceramic plates we use for the entrees, balancing them up my arm, walking back and forth from the hot line in the kitchen out to the dining room, and I am smiling at all my tables. I am doing the whole upbeat greeting routine, introducing myself, asking about their evening, laughing at their little jokes about the menu. But I am only smiling because I am supposed to, because my job and my tips literally depend on me looking happy and accommodating for the guests. I am not smiling because I actually feel anything good. Inside, I don't feel anything good at all. 

It is just that heavy emptiness, day after day. So even if the condo problem was completely resolved by tomorrow morning, I really think this feeling would still be there, just weighing me down while I am pouring water and clearing off tables. It is like it has become my normal state of being now, not just a reaction to the real estate, if that makes any sense.
Do you often feel worthless?

Worthless... yeah. Yeah, I really do. Honestly, that’s a huge part of why I finally came in to see you. I just... I keep having this overwhelming feeling that I’ve completely let my family down by taking on this mortgage. It was my push, you know? I wanted us to have our own place, to stop renting, to build equity, all that adult stuff you're supposed to do. My wife trusted me on it. And now look at the situation I've put us in. 

And it’s gotten to the point where that feeling just infects everything else, especially my shifts at the restaurant. It's like every single small mistake I make at work just becomes this massive, undeniable proof that I’m completely useless. 

Just the other night, for example, during the dinner rush—maybe around seven-thirty, the dining room was completely packed—I had this four-top by the window. Nice people. They asked for a side of our house-made garlic aioli for their fries. It’s a basic request, Waiter 101. But the kitchen was totally in the weeds, the expeditor was yelling for food runners to take hot plates, and I just got distracted and completely forgot to ring in the sauce. 

By the time I remembered and went back to check on them, they had already finished their food. And I know, logically, forgetting a two-ounce ramekin of mayonnaise is not the end of the world. It happens a dozen times a shift to everyone. But standing there at the computer terminal, it didn't feel small at all. It felt like this glaring evidence that I can't do anything right. My brain just immediately went to, 'You can't even remember a side of sauce, how are you ever going to handle this mortgage? How are you supposed to provide for your wife?' 

It just spirals like that all the time now. Every time I drop a fork on the floor, or if I accidentally ring in a regular Coke instead of a Diet Coke, it just hits me like a ton of bricks. It just makes me feel like I absolutely deserve whatever happens to me, like I deserve all this financial stress and panic because I'm just fundamentally incompetent and I'm the one who messed everything up for us.
Have other people noticed that you’ve been moving or speaking more slowly than usual?

Yeah, actually... it's funny you ask that, because my manager, Dave, he actually pulled me aside just the other day to ask if I was feeling alright. Because apparently, I’ve been doing this thing where I just... well, it goes two different ways, really. Sometimes I get this weird, trapped energy and I'm just pacing. We have this main aisle in the dining room, right between the booths and the freestanding tables, and I guess I was just walking up and down it, over and over, checking the exact same tables. Like, I’d go over and look at the printed receipts I’d already dropped off in those little black leather check presenters. I’d open the book, look at the receipt, close it, walk away, and then two minutes later I'm right back there doing it again, just pacing a hole in the floor. Dave was like, 'Man, you're making the guests dizzy, what are you looking for?' And I didn't even realize I was doing it. 

But then, on the flip side of that—and this is what really messes up my flow during a dinner rush—sometimes I get the exact opposite. I just get so incredibly bogged down. Like, I'll get so slowed down that even the simplest things take forever. The host will seat a new table in my section, and I know I need to go greet them. We keep these heavy, faux-leather menus stacked up at the host stand by the front doors. And I'll just be standing there, staring at the stack, and it takes me what feels like ten times longer than it normally should just to reach out, grab a couple of menus, and walk the twenty feet over to the table. 

Or I'll be walking to the POS—the computer terminal where we punch in the orders, ours is tucked back in this little alcove near the bar area—and my legs just feel like they're
Has this slowing down or pacing been happening nearly every day?

Yeah, pretty much every single day now. It's... it's really starting to become a constant thing, which is why Dave brought it up, I guess. Because it's not just a one-off bad shift where I'm a little scattered or tired. It's like, every time I clock in, I know I'm either going to be that guy who's wearing out the carpet by the booths, just pacing up and down, checking the same black leather check presenters over and over again—which I know is super annoying for the guests, because nobody wants their server hovering like a vulture when they're trying to figure out the tip—or I'm going to be the guy who looks like he's walking through wet cement just trying to get from the host stand to the POS terminal. 

And it's really frustrating because I know the layout of this restaurant like the back of my hand. I've walked those aisles thousands of times. I know exactly how many steps it takes to get from the kitchen double doors to table 42. But lately, almost every day, it's like my brain and my body are just completely disconnected. I'm either wired with this nervous energy that makes me loop around my section checking receipts I already dropped, or I'm so heavy and sluggish that even just picking up those thick menus and walking over to greet a new table feels like a monumental task. Dave definitely notices it happening all the time now, and I know the other servers are probably looking at me like I'm losing my mind, because I used to be so fast on the floor.
Are you absolutely convinced that you deserve to be punished for what happened with the condo, even when other people tell you that isn’t true?

Yeah, I mean... absolutely. I know I mentioned this earlier, but that's really the whole reason I'm sitting here talking to you right now. I just... I can't shake this feeling that I have completely and utterly let my family down. It's like this heavy weight sitting right on my chest, all the time. 

My wife, Sarah, she tries to tell me it's not my fault, that the market changed, that we made the decision together. She'll sit there on the couch with me after a shift and say, 'Honey, we're in this together, it's just a mortgage, we'll figure it out.' But I can't hear it. I just can't believe her, because I know I was the one pushing for it. I was the one looking at Zillow every night, talking about equity and investing in our future and all that stuff. I just sleep right through it. 

So, no, getting to sleep isn't really an issue for me. The sleeping part is fine. It's more... it's the waking up part that's hard. Because the second I open my eyes in the morning, before I even sit up, my brain just instantly boots up and remembers the mortgage and the debt and the whole mess. And then that physical weight is just right back on my chest for the rest of the day. But the actual sleeping? No, I don't have any trouble with that. I'm just too wiped out to stay awake.
